title: A measurement noise scaling law for cellular representation learning - Nature Machine Intelligence
byline: Gowri; Gokul; Sadalski; Igor; Raviv; Dan; Yin; Peng; Rosenfeld; Jonathan; Klein; Allon
html:
Abstract

Large genomic and imaging datasets can be used to train models that learn meaningful representations of cellular systems. Across domains, model performance improves predictably with dataset size and compute budget, providing a basis for allocating data and computation. Scientific data, however, are also limited by noise arising from factors such as molecular undersampling, sequencing errors and image resolution. Here we introduce mutual information with auxiliary signals as a metric of representation model performance and study its scaling with noise. By fitting more than 2,000 representation learning models across three data modalities (gene expression, sequence and image data), we show that noise defines a distinct axis along which performance improves. Noise scaling follows a logarithmic law. We derive the law from a model of noise propagation, and use it to define noise sensitivity and model capacity as benchmarking metrics. We show that protein-sequence representations tolerate error rates in modern sequencing data, whereas single-cell transcriptomic models remain noise limited at current measurement signal-to-noise ratio levels. Within transcriptomic cell-state representation learning models, we find that transformer-based models are more noise robust but less performant than variational autoencoders. Noise scaling metrics may support future model evaluation and experimental design.

Main

Cellular profiles obtained by single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and high-content imaging now span diverse tissues, developmental stages, disease states and experimental perturbations1,2. These large datasets (collectively, >108 samples) create opportunities to identify shared cellular states across experimental contexts and predict responses to novel perturbations3,4. To realize these opportunities, representation learning models are used to capture biologically meaningful variation and filter out technical nuisance factors5. Several deep learning approaches underlie such models so far, including transformer-based architectures, autoencoder-based architectures and models with contrastive losses6,7,8,9.

In domains outside of biology including natural language processing, image processing and chemical informatics, large model development has been guided by the study of model scalability. Choices in architecture, data acquisition and training strategies are guided by deep learning scaling laws, which are empirical relationships that describe how model performance improves with increases in key resources like data, compute and model parameters10,11,12,13,14,15.

In biology and other scientific domains, model performance can also be limited by noise in the data used for model training. A few specific data modalities, such as DNA sequence, exist in large repositories with reasonably low error rates (<10−2 errors per nucleotide16), but the majority of biological data modalities are more prone to measurement noise. scRNA-seq and spatially resolved transcriptomics, for example, are methods fundamentally limited by the low numbers of mRNA molecules per gene in each cell. Though measurement sensitivity has increased substantially with the ongoing development of these methods17, for many existing technologies, the probability of detecting a given mRNA molecule is well below 50%, and in some cases, the detection rate is further decreased by insufficient sequencing depth18. As a result, the measured transcript counts are subject to undersampling noise. Fluorescence microscopy is also prone to noise of different types including shot noise, scattering, out-of-focus light, autofluorescence, and limits in optical and camera resolution19.

In contrast to the scaling of model performance with dataset size and model size, much less is known about the role of measurement noise on the ability of a model to learn meaningful representations. In textual representation by large language models, errors in training data lead to degraded performance, predicted to persist even in the limit of infinite data20. However, textual data used in large language model training can be curated and are subject to extensive quality control21. As representation learning models are being developed for diverse biological tasks, understanding how noise alters the performance of models could support model evaluation, and allow the rational planning of data generation campaigns.

Here we show evidence for a general and quantitative scaling relationship between measurement noise and model performance across representation learning models of scRNA-seq, spatial transcriptomics, protein sequences and imaging data. We show that the noise scaling law can be derived by analogy to additive Gaussian noise channels, and that the resulting analytical form of the law can be used to define model benchmarks and identify noise sensitivity and saturation. Noise scaling may also guide experimental design. Critically evaluating several models, we find that a transformer-based transcriptomics model is more robust to noise but has lower saturating performance than a variational autoencoder, illustrating how noise scaling can inform both model choice and the design of data generation efforts.

Results

A metric for representation learning model performance

In deep learning scaling analyses, it is typical to evaluate model quality directly by measuring loss on held-out validation data10,11,12,14. However, loss has two key limitations as a metric. First, it is not comparable between models with different loss functions, or even for a single model applied to data with different statistical properties (for example, different noise properties)22. Second, even where losses are comparable, a lower loss need not translate into more useful representations for downstream tasks23,24.

To study the effect of noise on representation learning model performance and to avoid these issues, we introduce an alternative approach to measure the representation quality: estimating the mutual information (MI) between a model’s learned representation Z and an auxiliary signal Y, which consists of some information about each sample that remains hidden until after learning is completed (Fig. 1). We use a neural-network-based MI estimator that accommodates continuous and high-dimensional auxiliary signals25 and is consistent with well-established estimators on low-dimensional data (Supplementary Text VII). This yields a performance metric that is comparable across model types and noise levels within a given dataset. Because Z need not perfectly reconstruct Y, the approach tolerates some noise in Y at the cost of a lower maximum MI between Y and Z.

a, Workflow used to evaluate representation model quality as a function of noise, with model performance quantified by auxiliary MI (see the main text). The process is repeated across many noise levels (SNR η) to generate empirical noise scaling curves. b, Summary of the auxiliary signals, model families and noising processes used for each of the three data modalities in this study.

Formally, this approach generalizes linear probing26,27, and indeed, the MI values we report later in the text agree well with goodness of fit from linear probing (average Kendall rank correlation, τ = 0.71; Supplementary Text VI and Supplementary Fig. 8). We favour MI over linear probing for its general advantages as a metric: it captures nonlinear relationships and expresses representation quality in the standard units of bits. As with any probe-based approach, however, this metric is agnostic to variation in the measurement unrelated to Y, and therefore, it is not a universal measure of representation quality, but rather, one tied to a particular downstream task.

We first evaluated the representation model performance for four single-cell transcriptomic datasets, each of which provides an additional auxiliary signal as follows:

  • 1.

    Developmental time of ~107 cells profiled by scRNA-seq across mouse development, where developmental time is quantified by embryonic stage28.

  • 2.

    Surface protein abundances of ~105 peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) measured by an antibody panel through CITE-seq29.

  • 3.

    Transcriptional profile of a clonally related cell in ~105 mouse hematopoietic stem cells measured using lineage-traced scRNA-seq30.

  • 4.

    Transcriptional profile of a spatially adjacent cell in a coronal mouse brain section of ~105 cells measured using MERFISH31.

For each of these, we evaluated two linear baseline models: random projection, motivated as a representation learning baseline by the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma32, and dimensionality reduction by principal component analysis (PCA). We then evaluated three modern generative models with distinct architectures: single-cell variational inference (scVI)33, Geneformer6 and STATE34. scVI is a variational autoencoder designed to compress high-dimensional gene expression information into a low-dimensional latent space, with an explicit treatment of gene expression noise. Geneformer instead uses a transformer-based language model that maps gene expression vectors to sequences by ordering gene-specific tokens based on the expression level. STATE is a more recent transformer-based model that uses a different token embedding framework built on protein language models. Our implementations of scVI and Geneformer comprised 1.3–116.8 million and 1.9–13.5 million parameters, respectively (depending on the gene number in each dataset), and our STATE models comprised 5.4 million trainable parameters, although we note that parameter counts across different model families are not directly comparable. We trained Geneformer across multiple GPUs using DeepSpeed35. Model implementation and data preprocessing details are provided in the Methods.

In all cases, to facilitate consistent comparisons, we learned representations on one data subset, and then evaluated the performance in a separate, fixed held-out subset. This approach ensures that the observed differences in MI are attributable to variations in the representations themselves, rather than estimation artifacts.

Cell number scaling for cellular representations

As a baseline for understanding the impact of noise on model learning, we first established that the auxiliary MI performance I shows expected scaling behaviour with the number of samples N (here the number of single cells) used in training. In image and language models, it has been empirically observed that performance scales as a saturating power law with respect to the sample number14. For scRNA-seq data, model performance has similarly been shown to saturate with the dataset size36. For neural-network-based models (scVI, Geneformer and STATE), we observe that I is empirically well-described by a saturating power law across auxiliary tasks, \(I(N)={I}_{\infty }-{(N/{N}_{{\rm{sat}}})}^{-s}\), where the parameters I∞, Nsat and s characterize how each model learns from new data (mean fit coefficient of determination R2 = 0.90 across n = 120 models). The fits for these models are shown across datasets in Fig. 2a,b (Supplementary Fig. 4 shows the individually plotted curves), with parameter values and model comparisons shown in Supplementary Text II and Supplementary Fig. 3. The performance of PCA does not meaningfully fit the saturating power law as it saturates almost immediately with respect to the cell number, as also observed in prior work36. Thus, the MI performance metric that we will use recreates the well-studied sample size scaling: it recapitulates scaling and saturation, and recapitulates the observation that linear models have earlier saturation points than deep learning approaches.

Noise scaling for cellular representations

Although deep learning models are often thought to be strong denoisers37, the degree to which cellular representation learning models are robust to noise in their training data is unknown. A noise-robust model would exhibit a regime in which the informativity of learned representations remains stable despite increasing noise levels. We evaluated the extent to which models are noise robust by simulating increasing measurement noise through downsampling observed transcript counts and, subsequently, evaluating the quality of the learned representations of noisy data using auxiliary MI performance.

The dependence of model performance I on the degree of downsampling noise is shown in Fig. 2c. As expected, reducing the depth per cell degrades the performance of all models, across all datasets. Of note, no model or dataset exhibits large regimes of noise robustness. Instead, many of the measured performance curves are sigmoidal, with a short saturation span indicating only limited robustness at the transcript levels present in the original datasets before performance steadily deteriorates (Fig. 2c). A subset of the curves (for example, PCA representations for spatial information) remains unsaturated, indicating negligible robustness to downsampling noise, even at full transcript levels.

The smooth, sigmoidal performance curves as a function of downsampling noise suggest that a simple analytical relationship might capture how measurement noise constrains biological representation learning. Such a relationship would be valuable for experimental design, enabling the principled allocation of sequencing depth and cell numbers in the same way that neural scaling laws guide resource decisions in large-scale machine learning, as well as clarifying how different sources of noise impact model performance. By inspection, it is evidently not a power law, unlike previous neural scaling laws14.

To define the noise-performance relationship, we turned to a simple model of information loss in noisy communication channels (Box 1).
